## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.05397.030](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.05397.030)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “A molecular tweezer antagonizes seminal amyloids and HIV infection” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Randy Schekman (Senior editor) and three reviewers, one of whom, Jeffery W Kelly, is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

All reviewers concur that the significance of the work is potentially there. The concerns center around some of the data and critical control experiments relevant to the mechanism that seem to be missing.

All three reviewers expressed concerns centered around the mechanism of action of CRL01.

The authors postulate that classic host-guest complexes are forming whereas the reviewers suspect colloidal aggregation on the part of the CLR01 itself. Colloidal aggregation of organic small molecules can disrupt protein fibrils, by protein sequestration by the colloid (Feng et al., Nature Chem. Biol., 2008). Such a mechanism must be controlled for, especially given the peculiar efficacy of the compounds against the virion membranes themselves. Second, the authors should look to see if free lysine competes for CLR01 binding, disrupting its ability to act on the fibrils and the virions. There are few statistical analyses performed, so the relevance of comparing EC50 values is often unclear. On top of that, many of the raw data sets are of too low quality to produce accurate EC50 values, e.g. the lack of a saturation plateau. All three reviews are pasted below and the questions and suggestions in the reviews should be addressed if the authors choose to submit a revised manuscript.

Reviewer #1:

These results appear to be incredible, and they may be. There are several critical controls that appear to be lacking, as indicated below. If the data hold up after these controls, then I am enthusiastic. Amyloid fibrils in seminal fluid composed of at least 4 cationic proteins are established to enhance HIV transmission through intercourse by binding virons augmenting fusion efficiency. The Lys-binding molecular tweezer CLR01 delays the aggregation of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) fibrillization, half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of CLR01 inhibition exhibited were 2.6 μM and 18.8 μM, respectively. By contrast, the IC50 to impede PAP85-120 assembly was significantly higher at 970 μM. Have the authors controlled for the possibility that CLR01 is functioning through colloid formation? It is important that the authors show that CLR01 is not impeding the adsorption of the aggregates to the EM grid, which can distort what is in solution. If these reactions are run for more than 30h, does aggregation into fibrils eventually occur? Does seeded aggregation eventually occur? The critical control that CLR01 is not displacing ThT from the fibrils needs to be performed. The analog in which all eight lysine and arginine residues are replaced by alanine appears to be far from a perfect control in that this variant is anticipated to be much more amyloidogenic? In Figure 3, the critical control that CLR01 is not displacing ThT from the fibrils and inhibiting fibril adsorption to the grids needs to be run-the rapidity of disassembly is surprising, is it really disassembly? The result that CLR01 destroys retroviral particles with IC50 values between 10-20 μM by compromising virion integrity further suggests that CLR01 might be functioning as a colloid. CLR01 decreased viral infectivity of semen in a concentration-dependent manner, while CLR03 had no impact on semen-mediated infection enhancement. At a CLR01 concentration of 31 μM, the enhancing effect of semen was completely abolished. Thus, CLR01 prevents HIV infection in the presence of semen. If this is occuring through monomeric CLR01 this is incredible, but I suspect the authors' inhibitor is a micelle or colloid. The data are so impressive that I am concerned that these results are unlikely due to the monomeric molecular tweezer, but my hypothesis could be incorrect.

Reviewer #2:

Seminal amyloids are known to concentrate HIV virions and enhance infectivity. In this report, the authors use a recently identified, general inhibitor of amyloid formation (the molecular tweezer CLR01) to understand whether it also inhibits model seminal amyloids: SEVI, PAP85-120 and SEM1. CLR01 is known to work by docking to exposed lysine and arginine residues and this molecule has found use as a probe for biophysical chemistry and protein folding studies. Lump et al. first test CLR01 as a possible inhibitor of seminal amyloids in vitro, using EM and a ThT assay. They then test whether the molecules can reverse pre-formed amyloids using similar methods. Next, they test whether CLR01 might block binding of mock virions to fibrils and find that the compound seems to disrupt virions themselves. They use AFM and microscopy in vesicles and virus particles to test this idea – concluding that CLR01 seems to disrupt virion membranes, similar to a detergent. Somehow, this membrane disruption effect seems to be exclusive to viral membranes, but the mechanism remains cloudy (and somewhat confusing). They find that CLR01 blocks the infectivity-enhancing activity of seminal fibrils, both with and without addition of BSA. Based on these results, the possibility of using CLR01 for the prevention of viral spread are discussed. However, there are concerns (and even contradictions) about the lack of mechanistic knowledge and the nature of the CLR01-amyloid interaction is not well understood. The null hypotheses – that CLR01 is a non-specific lysine interactor or even a detergent – are not adequately tested. Without deeper mechanistic insight and more rigorous exploration of the binding events, publication of the work seems premature.

1) There are few statistical analyses performed, so the relevance of comparing EC50 values is often unclear. On top of that, many of the raw data sets are of too low quality to produce accurate values. For example, the value of 970 uM (Figure 2E) has no saturation plateau, so one assumes that the value has a very large error. Similar problems can be seen in the raw data for Figure 2F, Figure 2J, Figure 3G, Figure 3H and all of Figure 5. These results cannot be adequately fit because of sparse datapoints, so comparing (or even reporting) the half-maximal values is not advised.

2) One of the major problems with the manuscript is the uncertain mechanism of the compounds and the selectivity of the recognition. If CLR01 is simply blocking cationic charge of lysine and arginine residues, as the zeta potential and all-alanine mutant results imply, than one could presumably achieve this outcome faster, cheaper and more effectively with abundant biological polyanions, such as heparin or nucleic acids (DNA/RNA). What is the effect of these biological polyanions on the assembly of seminal amyloids and infectivity?

3) The hypothesis of CLR01 binding to individual lysine and arginine residues is not experimentally tested outside of a rather crude comparison of an all-alanine replacement peptide (which likely doesn't conform to the same structure as the native peptide). Does free lysine, arginine or other free organic cations (or even divalent cations) compete for CLR01 binding? Does systematic replacements of lysine residues would provide insight into what the key interactions might be? What is the affinity of these interactions? Presumably there are countless free lysine residues in true seminal fluid, so how can CLR01 have the selectivity required to identify the seminal amyloids (especially given the rather weak EC50 values in the mid-micromolar)?

4) The ability of the compounds to block fibril-induced virion activity in the presence of BSA doesn't appear to make logical sense. CLR01 was created as a general lysine/arginine probe – so why wouldn't the compound be adsorbed onto the surface of BSA, which carries surface-exposed nucleophiles? The affinity of CLR01 for the seminal amyloid peptides and BSA (as a stand-in for biological fluids) needs to be carefully performed – by NMR, ITC or other method.

5) The lack of CLR01-induced toxicity in mammalian cells is confusing, given the effects on vesicles and virion membranes (Figure 6). The mammalian cells have numerous cholesterol-rich, raft-like domains, so that argument doesn't work. Presumably, the mammalian membranes would be disrupted just like in the vesicle and virion studies, but not leading to toxicity. What is going on here? Is calcium flux activated? Do the cells change shape? What is the affinity of CLR01 for viral membranes, vesicles and mammalian membranes? What lipid is being bound? By what mechanism do the membranes dissolve? Normally, such questions could be addressed in subsequent work, but the readers of this document would be expected to have major concerns about the logical gas and contradictions in the datasets, making careful and unbiased discussion an important requirement.

6) What is the CMC equivalent of CLR01? In other words, at what concentration does it form micro-aggregates or micelles? Some (perhaps many?) of the observed activities could be a result of non-specific activities, as described by the Shoicet group. DLS studies and detergent competition experiments need to be performed.

Reviewer #3:

Lump and colleagues describe the activity of a host-guest cavitand-like molecule, CLR01, in disassembling seminal protein fibrils and directly disrupting the membrane of HIV (and related) virions, much reducing HIV virus infectivity. The cavitand-like CLR01 acts by binding to lysine or arginine amino acids (the guests), with previously measured affinities in the 20 μM range, and presumably this activity is what leads to de-fibrilization (although exactly why binding should lead to defibrilization is unclear; presumably binding is improved in the soluble form, though this is not stated in the manuscript). In principle this is an interesting story, and certainly a novel use of a cavitand-like molecule, one that might inspire other efforts to repurpose such molecules, which are well-known to chemists, for similar effects. The manuscript could have substantial impact. Before it is published, I suggest the authors address the following concerns:

1) My major concern regards the mechanism of action. The authors postulate that classic host-guest complexes are forming with the cationic amino acids, as shown in Figure 1B, and this is important to the specificity and ultimate usefulness of the compounds. Currently, however, the manuscript lacks two controls that would help establish this mechanism:

A) First, the authors should control for colloidal aggregation on the part of the CLR01 itself. Colloidal aggregation of organic small molecules can disrupt protein fibrils, by protein sequestration in the small molecule colloid (Feng et al., Nature Chem. Biol., 2008). Such a mechanism must be controlled for, especially given the peculiar efficacy of the compounds against the virion membranes themselves (this is hard to square with a host-guest type interaction, but would make sense for colloidal aggregates). To do so, the authors should do one or more of the following i. Look to see if CLR01 is forming colloids in the 10 - 30 μM range, for instance by dynamic light scattering. ii. Add a mild, non-ionic detergent such as Tween-100 to disrupt the colloidal aggregates. This would right-shift the efficacy curves (assuming the detergent doesn't disrupt the fibrils directly). iii. Before addition to the fibrils, spin down the aqueous “solution” of CRL01 (not the DMSO one) in a microfuge at its highest speed for 20 minutes. Use the supernatant as the CLR01 solution for efficacy testing (colloids will typically pellet over this time). iv. Add 10 mg/ml BSA to the fibril mixture, before addition of CLR01. BSA will prophylacticly coat colloids, disrupting their actions.

B) Second, the authors should look to see if free lysine competes for CLR01 binding, disrupting its ability to act on the fibrils and the virions. If it does not, or the effect is small, this would cast doubt on the mechanism proposed by the authors. This to me is an obvious control, and I worry that it was in the manuscript and I just overlooked it – if I did I apologize. If not, it should be done.

Both controls should be done for both the effects on the protein fibrils and on the direct effects of the virus membrane. Whereas I hesitate to put authors to more work, I believe that these controls will substantially strengthen the manuscript, and should take more than a few days to perform.

2) Minor points:

A) I thought many of the dose response curves could be higher in quality, and should be re-done at better resolution.

B) In the third paragraph of the subsection “CLR01 disaggregates preformed SEVI and PAP85-120 fibrils” the authors write that CLR01 acts sub-stoichiometrically. How do they know what the concentration of the relevant fibril species is? What is the stoichiometry?

C) In the Discussion, the authors speculate on the use of CLR01 in vivo, as a drug or drug lead. Probably the only way such a molecule could be used is topically. It will not be orally absorbed (in all likelihood), and an intravenous route would lead to low compliance. If they are to speculate on this, as they do now, they should alert the readership to these points.

D) I was unconvinced by the Concentration-Response curves, which are crucial to the efficacy arguments for CLR01. For Figure 2D, the curve should go through 0 (not 25%...how is this possible at no compound?). More observations are needed in the transition region, and the authors should certainly sample every half-log, not every log10 in concentration. For Figure 2J, they should calculate a curve that actually goes through their points. I assume they fixed the Hill coefficient to 1, which doesn't seem to be supported by the curve. Here too, they need more points. In Figure 5, the Y-axis of the concentration-response curves should be on a linear scale, not a log scale. If it were, the reader would quickly notice that the curves are quite steep, which can be informative, and sometimes concerning.

Notwithstanding these concerns, the manuscript is interesting and could have wide impact. If the authors can address the concerns of the missing controls, I would support its publication.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Münch et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010).

claims.claim: CLR01 is a 'molecular tweezer' specific for lysine and arginine residues.
claims.source: In this study, we establish that CLR01, a 'molecular tweezer' specific for lysine and arginine residues, inhibits the formation of infectivity-enhancing seminal amyloids and remodels preformed fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Fokkens et al., 2005; Klärner et al., 2006, 2010).

claims.claim: CLR01 inhibits the formation of infectivity-enhancing seminal amyloids.
claims.source: In this study, we establish that CLR01, a 'molecular tweezer' specific for lysine and arginine residues, inhibits the formation of infectivity-enhancing seminal amyloids and remodels preformed fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: CLR01 remodels preformed seminal amyloid fibrils.
claims.source: In this study, we establish that CLR01, a 'molecular tweezer' specific for lysine and arginine residues, inhibits the formation of infectivity-enhancing seminal amyloids and remodels preformed fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: CLR01 abrogates semen-mediated enhancement of viral infection by preventing the formation of virion–amyloid complexes.
claims.source: Moreover, CLR01 abrogates semen-mediated enhancement of viral infection by preventing the formation of virion–amyloid complexes and by directly disrupting the membrane integrity of HIV and other enveloped viruses.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: CLR01 directly disrupts the membrane integrity of HIV and other enveloped viruses.
claims.source: Moreover, CLR01 abrogates semen-mediated enhancement of viral infection by preventing the formation of virion–amyloid complexes and by directly disrupting the membrane integrity of HIV and other enveloped viruses.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 5, 6, and 8.

claims.claim: CLR01 acts by binding to target lysine and arginine residues rather than by a non-specific, colloidal mechanism.
claims.source: We establish that CLR01 acts by binding to the target lysine and arginine residues rather than by a non-specific, colloidal mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments including lysine/poly-L-lysine competition assays and biophysical characterization in Figure 7.

claims.claim: CLR01 counteracts both host factors important for HIV transmission and the pathogen itself.
claims.source: CLR01 counteracts both host factors that may be important for HIV transmission and the pathogen itself.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing effects on both seminal amyloids (host factors) and HIV virions (pathogen).

claims.claim: The combined anti-amyloid and antiviral activities make CLR01 a promising topical microbicide for blocking infection by HIV and other sexually transmitted viruses.
claims.source: These combined anti-amyloid and antiviral activities make CLR01 a promising topical microbicide for blocking infection by HIV and other sexually transmitted viruses.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The majority of new HIV-1 infections are transmitted via sexual intercourse.
claims.source: The majority of new HIV-1 infections are transmitted via sexual intercourse, and semen is the main vector for viral spread.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Semen potently enhances HIV infectivity.
claims.source: Far from being a passive vehicle, semen potently enhances HIV infectivity (Münch et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: HIV-enhancing activity of semen is attributed to seminal amyloid fibrils.
claims.source: This HIV-enhancing activity is attributed to seminal amyloid fibrils (Münch et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010; Roan et al., 2011; Usmani et al., 2014) that form by self-assembly of proteolytic fragments of prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP248-286 and PAP85-120) and the homologous proteins semenogelin 1 (SEM1) and semenogelin 2 (SEM2) (Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2012; Castellano and Shorter, 2012; Münch et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Seminal amyloid fibrils form by self-assembly of proteolytic fragments of prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP248-286 and PAP85-120) and semenogelin 1 (SEM1) and semenogelin 2 (SEM2).
claims.source: This HIV-enhancing activity is attributed to seminal amyloid fibrils (Münch et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010; Roan et al., 2011; Usmani et al., 2014) that form by self-assembly of proteolytic fragments of prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP248-286 and PAP85-120) and the homologous proteins semenogelin 1 (SEM1) and semenogelin 2 (SEM2) (Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2012; Castellano and Shorter, 2012; Münch et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Seminal amyloid fibrils are highly cationic.
claims.source: Seminal amyloid fibrils are highly cationic, and the positively charged fibrils capture HIV virions, increase viral attachment rates to target cells, and augment fusion (Roan et al., 2009; Arnold et al., 2012; Usmani et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Positively charged seminal amyloid fibrils capture HIV virions, increase viral attachment rates to target cells, and augment fusion.
claims.source: Seminal amyloid fibrils are highly cationic, and the positively charged fibrils capture HIV virions, increase viral attachment rates to target cells, and augment fusion (Roan et al., 2009; Arnold et al., 2012; Usmani et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Seminal amyloid fibrils promote HIV infection in vitro by several orders of magnitude.
claims.source: By doing so, fibrils promote HIV infection in vitro by several orders of magnitude, whereas the corresponding monomeric peptides have no effect (Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Monomeric seminal peptides have no effect on HIV infection.
claims.source: By doing so, fibrils promote HIV infection in vitro by several orders of magnitude, whereas the corresponding monomeric peptides have no effect (Münch et al., 2007; Roan et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The stimulatory effect of seminal amyloid is greatest at low virus concentrations.
claims.source: Importantly, the stimulatory effect of seminal amyloid is the greatest at low virus concentrations (Münch et al., 2007), and semen and PAP248-286 fibrils (termed SEVI for Semen-derived Enhancer of Virus Infection) may facilitate vaginal virus transmission after exposure to low viral doses (Miller et al., 1994; Neildez et al., 1998; Münch et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Semen and PAP248-286 fibrils (SEVI) may facilitate vaginal virus transmission after exposure to low viral doses.
claims.source: Importantly, the stimulatory effect of seminal amyloid is the greatest at low virus concentrations (Münch et al., 2007), and semen and PAP248-286 fibrils (termed SEVI for Semen-derived Enhancer of Virus Infection) may facilitate vaginal virus transmission after exposure to low viral doses (Miller et al., 1994; Neildez et al., 1998; Münch et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: HIV transmission rates are relatively low, occurring as infrequently as 1 in 200 to as low as 1 in 10,000 coital acts.
claims.source: HIV transmission rates are relatively low, occurring as infrequently as 1 in 200 to as low as 1 in 10,000 coital acts (Gray et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Counteraction of infectivity promoting amyloids in semen should reduce or even prevent HIV transmission via the sexual route.
claims.source: Thus, counteraction of infectivity promoting amyloids in semen should reduce or even prevent HIV transmission via the sexual route.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference stated in the introduction based on the role of seminal amyloids in HIV transmission.

claims.claim: CLR01 inhibits amyloid fibrillization by engaging specific lysine, arginine, or both residues within a variety of disease-associated amyloidogenic proteins including amyloid-β protein (Aβ), tau, islet amyloid polypeptide, transthyretin, and α-synuclein.
claims.source: The lysine- and arginine-specific molecular tweezer, CLR01 (Figure 1A,B) (Fokkens et al., 2005; Klärner et al., 2006, 2010), inhibits amyloid fibrillization by engaging specific lysine, arginine, or both residues within a variety of disease-associated amyloidogenic proteins including amyloid-β protein (Aβ), tau, islet amyloid polypeptide, transthyretin, and α-synuclein (Sinha et al., 2011; Attar et al., 2012; Prabhudesai et al., 2012; Sinha et al., 2012; Acharya et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2014; Lopes et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: CLR01 has been found to slowly remodel preformed Aβ and α-synuclein fibrils over the course of several weeks.
claims.source: Furthermore, CLR01 has even been found to slowly remodel preformed Aβ and α-synuclein fibrils over the course of several weeks (Sinha et al., 2011; Prabhudesai et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: CLR01 binds lysine residues with a Kd of ∼10 µM.
claims.source: CLR01 binds lysine residues with a Kd of ∼10 µM and also binds arginine residues, albeit with ∼10-fold lower affinity (Fokkens et al., 2005; Dutt et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: CLR01 binds arginine residues with ∼10-fold lower affinity than lysine residues.
claims.source: CLR01 binds lysine residues with a Kd of ∼10 µM and also binds arginine residues, albeit with ∼10-fold lower affinity (Fokkens et al., 2005; Dutt et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The unprecedented high specificity of CLR01 for basic amino acids relies on a unique binding mode in which the tweezer draws the cationic side chains into its torus-shaped cavity and engages the ammonium cation of lysine or the guanidinium cation of arginine with its anionic phosphate group in a tight ion pair.
claims.source: The unprecedented high specificity of CLR01 for basic amino acids relies on a unique binding mode in which the tweezer draws the cationic side chains into its torus-shaped cavity and engages the ammonium cation of lysine or the guanidinium cation of arginine with its anionic phosphate group in a tight ion pair (Figure 1B) (Klärner and Schrader, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction, supported by a citation, and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: No other amino acids fulfill the requirements for the CLR01 threading mechanism.
claims.source: No other amino acids fulfill the requirements for this threading mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on the structural requirements for CLR01 binding.

claims.claim: The structure of the CLR01-lysine complex and the precise mechanism of lysine threading into the CLR01 guest cavity and subsequent ion pairing have been extensively characterized by NMR spectroscopy, crystal structure, molecular dynamics, and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations.
claims.source: The structure of the CLR01-lysine complex and the precise mechanism of lysine threading into the CLR01 guest cavity and subsequent ion pairing have been extensively characterized by NMR spectroscopy, crystal structure, molecular dynamics, and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations (Bier et al., 2013; Dutt et al., 2013; Klärner and Schrader, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claims.claim: CLR01 appears only to complex with readily accessible lysine or arginine residues on protein surfaces.
claims.source: Importantly, CLR01 appears only to complex with readily accessible lysine or arginine residues on protein surfaces, as evidenced by crystal structures and NMR experiments (Bier et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The restriction to accessible lysine or arginine residues makes CLR01 more selective for lysine or arginine residues found in intrinsically unfolded proteins or protein sequences.
claims.source: This restriction makes CLR01 more selective for lysine or arginine residues found in intrinsically unfolded proteins or protein sequences.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is a logical inference from the structural properties of CLR01.

claims.claim: Amyloidogenic seminal peptides are particularly rich in lysine and arginine residues.
claims.source: Since amyloidogenic seminal peptides are particularly rich in lysine and arginine residues (Roan et al., 2009; Arnold et al., 2012; Castellano and Shorter, 2012) (Figure 1C–E, Lys and Arg residues are highlighted in red), we hypothesized that CLR01 might interfere with their HIV-enhancing activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction, supported by citations, and illustrated in Figure 1C-E.

claims.claim: Lysine residues in PAP248-286, PAP85-120, SEM1, and SEM2 peptides are frequently found within or immediately adjacent to hexapeptides predicted to form self-complementary β-strands (steric zippers).
claims.source: Lysine residues in PAP248-286, PAP85-120, SEM1, and SEM2 peptides are frequently found within or immediately adjacent to hexapeptides predicted to form self-complementary β-strands (Figure 1C–E, underlined residues), termed steric zippers, which often comprise the spine of amyloid fibrils (Nelson et al., 2005; Goldschmidt et al., 2010; Sievers et al., 2011; Castellano and Shorter, 2012; Frohm et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section, supported by citations, and illustrated in Figure 1C-E.

claims.claim: In silico, CLR01 bound at least seven of the eight positively charged residues in PAP248-286 without grossly altering peptide secondary structure.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that in silico, CLR01 bound at least seven of the eight positively charged residues in PAP248-286 without grossly altering peptide secondary structure (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1F, based on computational modeling.

claims.claim: CLR01 engaged Lys251, Lys253, Lys281, and Lys282 in PAP248-286, which all reside in predicted steric zippers.
claims.source: Indeed, CLR01 engaged Lys251, Lys253, Lys281, and Lys282 (Figure 1F,G), which all reside in predicted steric zippers (Castellano and Shorter, 2012) (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figures 1C, 1F, and 1G, based on computational modeling.

claims.claim: CLR01 bound Arg257, Lys281, and Lys282 in PAP248-286, which form part of the cross-β SEVI fibril core defined by hydrogen–deuterium exchange.
claims.source: Moreover, CLR01 bound Arg257, Lys281, and Lys282 (Figure 1F,G), which form part of the cross-β SEVI fibril core defined by hydrogen–deuterium exchange (French and Makhatadze, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section, illustrated in Figures 1F and 1G, and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: CLR03 only established more distant and variable interactions with lysine and arginine residues in PAP248-286.
claims.source: By contrast, CLR03 only established more distant and variable interactions with lysine and arginine residues (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1G, based on computational modeling.

claims.claim: CLR01, but not CLR03, inhibited fibril assembly of PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107).
claims.source: Using the fluorescence of the diagnostic dye Thioflavin-T (ThT), which increases upon amyloid binding, we found that CLR01, but not CLR03, inhibited fibril assembly of all three peptides (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2A-C using ThT fluorescence assays.

claims.claim: The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of CLR01 inhibition of PAP248-286 fibrillization was ∼1.19 µM.
claims.source: The half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of CLR01 inhibition of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) fibrillization were ∼1.19 µM and ∼16.2 µM, respectively (Figure 2D,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The IC50 of CLR01 inhibition of SEM1(45-107) fibrillization was ∼16.2 µM.
claims.source: The half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50) of CLR01 inhibition of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) fibrillization were ∼1.19 µM and ∼16.2 µM, respectively (Figure 2D,F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The IC50 for inhibition of PAP248-286 fibrillization was significantly lower than the IC50 for inhibition of SEM1(45-107) fibrillization.
claims.source: The IC50 for inhibition of PAP248-286 fibrillization was significantly lower than the IC50 for inhibition of SEM1(45-107) fibrillization (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.0001), suggesting that lysine, arginine, or both residues are more critical for PAP248-286 fibrillization.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Lysine, arginine, or both residues are more critical for PAP248-286 fibrillization than for SEM1(45-107) fibrillization.
claims.source: The IC50 for inhibition of PAP248-286 fibrillization was significantly lower than the IC50 for inhibition of SEM1(45-107) fibrillization (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.0001), suggesting that lysine, arginine, or both residues are more critical for PAP248-286 fibrillization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the difference in IC50 values.

claims.claim: Inhibition of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) fibrillization by CLR01 exhibited shallow dose–response curves with Hill slopes of ∼0.6 for PAP248-286 and ∼0.44 for SEM1(45-107), indicating negative co-operativity or CLR01 binding to multiple sites with different affinities.
claims.source: Moreover, inhibition of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) fibrillization exhibited shallow dose–response curves with Hill slopes of ∼0.6 for PAP248-286 and ∼0.44 for SEM1(45-107) (Figure 2D,F), indicating negative co-operativity or CLR01 binding to multiple sites with different affinities.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2D and 2F.

claims.claim: The shallow dose response curves for CLR01 inhibition of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) fibrillization provide evidence against a non-specific mechanism of inhibition involving colloidal CLR01 aggregates.
claims.source: Importantly, these shallow dose responses provide evidence against a non-specific mechanism of inhibition involving colloidal CLR01 aggregates, as aggregating inhibitors tend to exhibit steep dose response curves (Shoichet, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The IC50 of CLR01 to impede PAP85-120 assembly was ∼228 µM.
claims.source: The IC50 of CLR01 to impede PAP85-120 assembly was significantly higher at ∼228 µM (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.0001; Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The higher IC50 for PAP85-120 is likely due to the lower number of lysine or arginine residues in the PAP85-120 sequence located in hexapeptides predicted to have high amyloid propensity.
claims.source: The higher IC50 is likely due to the lower number of lysine or arginine residues in the PAP85-120 sequence located in hexapeptides predicted to have high amyloid propensity (Figure 1D) (Castellano and Shorter, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by reference to Figure 1D and a citation.

claims.claim: PAP85-120 has 1 lysine or arginine located in predicted steric zippers, whereas PAP248-286 has 4 and SEM1(45-107) has 3.
claims.source: Indeed, PAP85-120 has 1 lysine or arginine located in predicted steric zippers, whereas PAP248-286 has 4 and SEM1(45-107) has 3 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be verified from Figure 1C-E.

claims.claim: The Hill slope for CLR01 inhibition of PAP85-120 assembly was ∼1.26, indicating weak positive co-operativity.
claims.source: The Hill slope was ∼1.26, indicating weak positive co-operativity (Figure 2E), but was still below the ∼1.5–2 range that might indicate a mechanism of inhibition involving colloidal CLR01 aggregates (Shoichet, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis confirmed that CLR01 prevented assembly of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) into mature fibrils.
claims.source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis confirmed that CLR01 prevented assembly of PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107) into mature fibrils (Figure 2A,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claims.claim: In the presence of CLR01, only small oligomeric forms or amorphous aggregates in combination with sparse short fibrils were detectable for PAP248-286 and SEM1(45-107).
claims.source: Only small oligomeric forms (Figure 2A) or amorphous aggregates in combination with sparse short fibrils (Figure 2C) were detectable in the presence of CLR01, as opposed to abundant fibrils observed in the presence of buffer or CLR03 (Figure 2A,C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claims.claim: The effect of CLR01 on PAP85-120 assembly was less apparent by TEM.
claims.source: The effect of CLR01 on PAP85-120 assembly was less apparent by TEM (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: PAP85-120 assemblies formed in the presence of CLR01 appeared more flexible and curvilinear, and differed from the rigid, straight fibrils formed in the presence of CLR03 or buffer.
claims.source: However, the PAP85-120 assemblies formed in the presence of CLR01 appeared more flexible and curvilinear, and differed from the rigid, straight fibrils formed in the presence of CLR03 or buffer (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The structures formed by PAP85-120 in the presence of CLR01 were not ThT-reactive and most likely represent non-amyloid aggregates.
claims.source: Since the structures that formed in the presence of CLR01 were not ThT-reactive (Figure 2B) they most likely represent non-amyloid aggregates.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the ThT data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: CLR01 appears to impede the transition of PAP85-120 to mature amyloid fibrils and abrogates formation of SEVI and SEM1(45-107) fibrils.
claims.source: Thus, CLR01 appears to impede the transition of PAP85-120 to mature amyloid fibrils and abrogates formation of SEVI and SEM1(45-107) fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the TEM and ThT data.

claims.claim: CLR01 was unable to block PAP248-286(Ala) fibrillization.
claims.source: PAP248-286(Ala) formed amyloid fibrils in the presence of CLR01, CLR03, and buffer (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In the presence of CLR01, PAP248-286(Ala) assembles into a subtly distinct set of cross-beta structures or fibril 'strains' that are less ThT-reactive.
claims.source: Thus, it is likely that in the presence of CLR01, PAP248-286(Ala) assembles into a subtly distinct set of cross-beta structures or fibril 'strains' that are less ThT-reactive (Figure 2G,H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figures 2G and 2H.

claims.claim: Amyloidogenesis by PAP85-120(Ala) was unaffected by CLR01.
claims.source: Amyloidogenesis by PAP85-120(Ala) was also unaffected by CLR01 (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: PAP248-286(Ala) and PAP85-120(Ala) peptides spontaneously assemble into amyloid more rapidly than the wild-type peptides.
claims.source: The PAP248-286(Ala) and PAP85-120(Ala) peptides spontaneously assemble into amyloid more rapidly than the wild-type peptides (Figure 2A,B,G,I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and can be observed by comparing the kinetics in Figures 2A, 2B, 2G, and 2I.

claims.claim: CLR01-lysine contacts, CLR01-arginine contacts, or both, are essential for inhibition of fibrillization.
claims.source: These findings suggest that CLR01-lysine contacts, CLR01-arginine contacts, or both, are essential for inhibition of fibrillization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the inability of CLR01 to inhibit fibrillization of alanine-substituted peptides.

claims.claim: Both 20 mM lysine and 1 mM poly-L-lysine completely abrogated CLR01 inhibition of fibril formation by PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107).
claims.source: Both 20 mM lysine and 1 mM poly-L-lysine completely abrogated CLR01 inhibition of fibril formation by these three peptides.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The results with lysine and poly-L-lysine strongly support direct interaction of the tweezer with lysine, arginine, or both residues in PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) as the underlying mechanism of CLR01 inhibition.
claims.source: These results strongly support direct interaction of the tweezer with lysine, arginine, or both residues in PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) as the underlying mechanism of CLR01 inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the competition experiments with lysine and poly-L-lysine.

claims.claim: CLR01 inhibited PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) fibril assembly in the presence of BSA (10 mg/ml) or when solutions containing CLR01 were centrifuged at 16,100×g for 20 min before adding the supernatant solution to the proteins.
claims.source: CLR01 was found to inhibit PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) fibril assembly in the presence of BSA (10 mg/ml) or when solutions containing CLR01 were centrifuged at 16,100×g for 20 min before adding the supernatant solution to the proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: CLR01 is not inhibiting PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) fibril assembly via a mechanism that involves colloidal CLR01 aggregates.
claims.source: Thus, CLR01 is not inhibiting PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) fibril assembly via a mechanism that involves colloidal CLR01 aggregates.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the BSA and centrifugation experiments.

claims.claim: CLR01 completely inhibited seeded PAP248-286 fibrillization.
claims.source: Remarkably, in addition to obstructing unseeded PAP248-286 assembly (Figure 2A), CLR01 also completely inhibited seeded fibrillization (Figure 2J,K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2J and 2K.

claims.claim: The IC50 of CLR01 for inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly was ∼15.3 µM.
claims.source: Dose–response analysis established an IC50 of ∼15.3 µM for CLR01 inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly (Figure 2L) compared to ∼1.19 µM for spontaneous PAP248-286 assembly (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2L.

claims.claim: Higher concentrations of CLR01 are required to inhibit PAP248-286 assembly once SEVI fibrils have formed.
claims.source: Thus, higher concentrations of CLR01 are required to inhibit PAP248-286 assembly once SEVI fibrils have formed.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the comparison of IC50 values for unseeded and seeded assembly.

claims.claim: The Hill slope for inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly was ∼3.1 indicating positive co-operativity.
claims.source: Interestingly, the Hill slope for inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly was ∼3.1 indicating positive co-operativity and was steeper than the Hill slope of ∼0.6 for inhibition of spontaneous PAP248-286 fibrillization (Figure 2D,L).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figures 2D and 2L.

claims.claim: Inhibition of seeded assembly by CLR01 was unaffected by BSA or by preclearing CLR01 solutions via centrifugation.
claims.source: However, this difference is not likely to be due colloidal CLR01 aggregates, as inhibition of seeded assembly by CLR01 was unaffected by BSA or by preclearing CLR01 solutions via centrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly was alleviated by excess lysine or poly-L-lysine.
claims.source: Inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly was alleviated by excess lysine or poly-L-lysine (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly by CLR01 likely requires specific interaction with lysine, arginine, or both residues.
claims.source: Thus, inhibition of seeded PAP248-286 assembly by CLR01 likely requires specific interaction with lysine, arginine, or both residues.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the competition experiments with lysine and poly-L-lysine.

claims.claim: CLR01 likely acts at multiple stages of the fibrillization process including the initial nucleation and fibril elongation steps.
claims.source: Importantly, because CLR01 impedes both unseeded and seeded PAP248-286 assembly, it likely acts at multiple stages of the fibrillization process including the initial nucleation and fibril elongation steps.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the ability of CLR01 to inhibit both unseeded and seeded assembly.

claims.claim: Lysine, arginine, or both residues play an important role in the primary nucleation and subsequent elongation of PAP248–286 fibrils.
claims.source: These observations also indicate that lysine, arginine, or both residues play an important role in the primary nucleation and subsequent elongation of PAP248–286 fibrils.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the effects of CLR01 on both unseeded and seeded assembly.

results.result: Semen is the main vector for HIV transmission and contains amyloid fibrils that enhance viral infection by several orders of magnitude, particularly at low virus concentrations. These fibrils are formed from proteolytic fragments of prostatic acid phosphatase and semenogelins, are highly cationic, and capture HIV virions to increase attachment and fusion with target cells.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C11-C21) establish the biological context for the study and are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work. The claims accurately represent established knowledge about seminal amyloids and their role in HIV transmission enhancement, providing the scientific rationale for investigating CLR01 as a potential intervention.

results.result: CLR01 is a lysine- and arginine-specific molecular tweezer that binds these residues with high specificity through a unique threading mechanism, inhibits amyloid fibrillization of various disease-associated proteins, and can slowly remodel preformed fibrils. CLR01 binds lysine with Kd ~10 µM and arginine with ~10-fold lower affinity, preferentially engaging accessible residues on protein surfaces.
results.evaluation: These claims (C3, C23-C31) about CLR01's properties and mechanism are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work and structural studies. The binding specificity, affinity values, and mechanism have been extensively characterized by NMR, crystallography, molecular dynamics, and QM/MM calculations as stated in C29.

results.result: Seminal amyloid peptides (PAP248-286, PAP85-120, SEM1) are rich in lysine and arginine residues that are frequently located within or adjacent to predicted steric zippers. Computational modeling shows that CLR01 binds at least seven of eight positively charged residues in PAP248-286, including residues in predicted steric zippers and the fibril core, while CLR03 establishes only distant and variable interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 are supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1C-E) and replica exchange molecular dynamics simulations (Figure 1F-G). The computational predictions provide a rational basis for testing CLR01's effects on seminal amyloid formation and are consistent with CLR01's known binding specificity.

results.result: CLR01, but not CLR03, inhibits spontaneous fibril assembly of PAP248-286, PAP85-120, and SEM1(45-107) with IC50 values of ~1.19 µM, ~228 µM, and ~16.2 µM respectively. The inhibition exhibits shallow dose-response curves (Hill slopes 0.44-1.26), and TEM confirms that CLR01 prevents mature fibril formation, instead producing oligomers, amorphous aggregates, or non-amyloid structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C54 are well-supported by ThT fluorescence assays (Figure 2A-F) and TEM imaging (Figure 2A-C). The IC50 values are quantified with appropriate replicates, statistical analysis is performed (one-way ANOVA), and the shallow Hill slopes provide evidence against colloidal aggregation mechanisms. The differential sensitivity correlates with lysine/arginine content in predicted steric zippers.

results.result: CLR01 cannot inhibit fibrillization of alanine-substituted peptides (PAP248-286(Ala) and PAP85-120(Ala)) where lysine and arginine residues are replaced with alanine, demonstrating that CLR01-lysine/arginine contacts are essential for inhibition of fibrillization.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by ThT and sedimentation assays (Figure 2G-I) showing that alanine substitution abolishes CLR01's inhibitory activity. This negative control experiment strongly supports the specificity of CLR01's mechanism and rules out non-specific effects, providing critical evidence for the proposed lysine/arginine-dependent mechanism.

results.result: Excess free lysine (20 mM) or poly-L-lysine (1 mM) completely abrogates CLR01 inhibition of fibril formation, and CLR01 retains activity in the presence of BSA or after centrifugation to remove potential aggregates, strongly supporting that CLR01 acts through direct interaction with lysine/arginine residues rather than via colloidal aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by competition experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and control experiments with BSA and centrifugation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). These experiments provide strong mechanistic evidence for specific lysine/arginine binding and rule out colloidal aggregation as the mechanism of action.

results.result: CLR01 completely inhibits seeded PAP248-286 fibrillization with IC50 ~15.3 µM (vs ~1.19 µM for unseeded), showing a steeper Hill slope (~3.1 vs ~0.6). The inhibition is unaffected by BSA or centrifugation but is alleviated by excess lysine/poly-L-lysine, indicating CLR01 acts at multiple stages of fibrillization including nucleation and elongation through specific lysine/arginine interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are supported by seeded assembly experiments (Figure 2J-L) and appropriate controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). The higher IC50 for seeded assembly is logical given that fibrils are already formed, and the mechanistic interpretation that CLR01 acts at multiple stages is reasonable based on its ability to inhibit both unseeded and seeded assembly.

results.result: CLR01 rapidly remodels preformed SEVI and PAP85-120 fibrils (>50% reduction in ThT fluorescence after 2 hr), confirmed by TEM showing few intact fibrils and predominantly smaller nonfibrillar species. SEM1(45-107) fibrils were not remodeled. This remodeling is remarkably rapid compared to weeks required for Aβ or α-synuclein fibrils, occurring on a timescale relevant for HIV prevention.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 are well-supported by ThT assays and TEM/confocal microscopy (Figure 3A-C). The rapid kinetics (2 hr) are clearly demonstrated and appropriately compared to prior work on other amyloids. The failure to remodel SEM1(45-107) fibrils is an important negative result that is honestly reported and provides specificity to the findings.

results.result: CLR01 treatment of SEVI fibrils causes loss of the β-sheet minimum by circular dichroism, confirming alteration of cross-β architecture. CLR01-remodeled SEVI fibrils are less effective seeds for polymerization of monomeric PAP248-286, indicating CLR01 remodels SEVI into alternative non-templating conformers.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by circular dichroism spectroscopy (Figure 3D-E) and seeding experiments (Figure 3F). The CD data directly demonstrate structural changes in the fibrils, and the reduced seeding capacity provides functional evidence that the remodeled structures are biochemically distinct from native fibrils.

results.result: CLR01 remodels SEVI and PAP85-120 fibrils with EC50 values of ~0.89 µM and ~1.41 µM respectively, with shallow dose-response curves (Hill slopes approximately -0.6 and -0.726). Remarkably, remodeling occurs at sub-stoichiometric concentrations relative to peptide monomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by dose-response experiments (Figure 3G-H). The EC50 values are well-quantified, and the shallow Hill slopes again argue against colloidal mechanisms. The sub-stoichiometric activity is particularly notable and suggests high efficiency, though the mechanism enabling this is not fully explained.

results.result: CLR01 cannot remodel preformed SEVI(Ala) or PAP85-120(Ala) fibrils, and excess lysine/poly-L-lysine prevents CLR01's remodeling activity. CLR01 retains activity in the presence of BSA or after centrifugation. These findings demonstrate that CLR01 remodels fibrils via specific binding to lysine/arginine residues, not through colloidal aggregates.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 are supported by experiments with alanine-substituted fibrils (Figure 3I-L), competition assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and BSA/centrifugation controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). These comprehensive controls provide strong evidence for the specificity of CLR01's mechanism in fibril remodeling, paralleling the evidence for inhibition of fibril formation.

results.result: CLR01, but not CLR03, rapidly neutralizes the positive surface charge of SEVI, PAP85-120, and SEM1(49-107) fibrils (within minutes by zeta potential). Pre-treatment with lysine/poly-L-lysine abrogates this activity. CLR01-treated fibrils cannot form complexes with virions and CLR01 displaces virions from preformed fibril-virion complexes without affecting virion fluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C101 are supported by zeta potential measurements (Figure 4A), competition experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and confocal microscopy (Figure 4B-D). The rapid charge neutralization provides a clear mechanism for preventing fibril-virion interactions, and the ability to displace pre-bound virions is particularly important for practical applications.

results.result: CLR01 and CLR03 show no cytotoxicity in TZM-bl cells up to 500 µM, unlike surfactants (Triton X-100, nonoxynol 9, SDS). SEVI, PAP85-120, and SEM1(49-107) enhance HIV infection 33-64 fold in a dose-dependent manner, but pretreatment with CLR01 (not CLR03) eliminates this infection-enhancing property.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 are supported by MTT cytotoxicity assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and HIV infection assays (Figure 4E). The lack of cytotoxicity is important for potential therapeutic applications, and the complete abrogation of infection enhancement demonstrates functional efficacy. The dose-dependent enhancement by amyloids is consistent with prior literature.

results.result: CLR01, but not CLR03, exhibits direct anti-HIV activity with IC50 values of ~13.7-20.1 µM against multiple HIV-1 strains (X4-tropic, R5-tropic, transmitted/founder viruses). The antiviral effect requires virion exposure to CLR01, not cell pretreatment, and is independent of viral co-receptor tropism or strain.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by dose-response experiments with multiple HIV-1 strains (Figure 5A) and cell vs. virion treatment experiments (Figure 5B). The broad activity across different strains and tropisms is well-demonstrated, and the requirement for virion exposure clearly indicates a direct antiviral mechanism rather than a cellular effect.

results.result: Pre-incubation of CLR01 with poly-L-lysine abrogates its anti-HIV activity in a dose-dependent manner (near-complete inhibition at 75 nM poly-L-lysine), demonstrating that the lysine-binding cavity is important for antiviral activity. CLR01's antiviral activity is unaffected by BSA (up to 5%) or centrifugation to remove aggregates, indicating colloidal aggregates do not contribute to antiviral activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C116 are supported by competition experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and BSA/centrifugation controls (Figure 5—figure supplements 2-4). These experiments provide strong evidence that the antiviral mechanism, like the anti-amyloid mechanism, depends on specific lysine binding rather than non-specific colloidal effects.

results.result: CLR01 treatment increases p24 in the soluble fraction of HIV samples and causes rapid loss of infectivity (62% reduction in 5 min, ~100% in 10 min with 10 µM CLR01). AFM confirms CLR01 destroys virion architecture of MLV and HIV-1 particles, including those lacking glycoproteins (Δenv), indicating CLR01 disrupts viral membrane integrity.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 are supported by p24 ELISA (Figure 6A), time-course infectivity assays (Figure 6B), and AFM imaging (Figure 6C-D). The rapid kinetics, p24 release, and AFM visualization of destroyed virions provide converging evidence for membrane disruption. The effect on Δenv particles is particularly important for demonstrating that the mechanism targets the membrane rather than glycoproteins.

results.result: Viral membranes are enriched 2-3 fold in sphingomyelin and cholesterol forming lipid rafts. CLR01 selectively permeabilizes model viral membranes (DOPC/SM/Chol) within 5-10 min while having no effect on DOPC membranes even after 60 min. AFM shows CLR01 induces changes in phase coexistence and eliminates distinct liquid-ordered and liquid-disordered domains in raft-containing membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C128 are supported by experiments with giant unilamellar vesicles (Figure 6E) and AFM of supported lipid bilayers (Figure 6F). The selective disruption of raft-containing membranes provides a mechanistic explanation for why CLR01 affects viral but not cellular membranes. The experimental design with appropriate controls (DOPC alone vs. DOPC/SM/Chol) is sound.

results.result: Comprehensive biophysical characterization shows CLR01 is predominantly monomeric under assay conditions. NMR shows very weak dimerization (Ka ~60 M⁻¹, ~5% dimers at 500 µM) in PBS but not in HEPES buffer. DOSY reveals hydrodynamic radii of ~0.9-1.0 nm. No critical micelle concentration was detected by pyrene fluorescence. DLS shows small particles (5-8 nm) at high concentrations in PBS but not the 95-400 nm size typical of colloidal aggregates. The vast majority of CLR01 molecules are monomeric, making colloidal aggregation highly unlikely to contribute to observed activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C141 are supported by multiple orthogonal biophysical techniques (NMR, DOSY, ITC, pyrene fluorescence, DLS) shown in Figure 7 and supplements. The comprehensive characterization using multiple methods provides strong evidence against colloidal aggregation. The buffer-dependent differences are noted and the quantitative measurements are appropriate. This extensive characterization addresses a critical concern about mechanism of action.

results.result: CLR01, but not CLR03, reduces infection rates of enveloped viruses HCMV, HSV-2, and HCV, but does not inhibit the non-enveloped adenovirus HAdV5. CLR01 is a broad-spectrum inhibitor of enveloped viruses, including sexually transmitted viruses (HIV-1, HSV-2, HCV).
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 are supported by infection assays with multiple viruses (Figure 8A-D). The selectivity for enveloped viruses is clearly demonstrated by the lack of effect on adenovirus, which is an important control. The broad-spectrum activity against diverse enveloped viruses supports the proposed membrane-disruption mechanism.

results.result: CLR01 maintains amyloid-remodeling activity in artificial semen simulant containing 50 mg/ml BSA. Seminal plasma enhances HIV infection 8-10 fold, and CLR01 decreases this enhancement in a concentration-dependent manner, completely abolishing the stimulatory effect at 31 µM. CLR01 prevents HIV infection in the presence of semen.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 are supported by experiments with artificial semen simulant (Figure 9A) and human seminal plasma (Figure 9B). These experiments are critical for demonstrating that CLR01 functions in the complex biological environment of semen, which is essential for potential clinical application. The dose-dependent effect and complete abolition of enhancement at 31 µM are well-demonstrated.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence establish that CLR01 acts through specific binding to lysine and arginine residues rather than by non-specific colloidal mechanisms: (1) alanine substitution abolishes activity, (2) excess lysine/poly-L-lysine competitively inhibits activity, (3) activity is retained with BSA or after centrifugation, (4) shallow dose-response curves, (5) comprehensive biophysical characterization shows predominantly monomeric CLR01 without colloidal aggregates.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic conclusion (claims C8, C44, C59, C61, C63, C70, C91, C93, C94, C112, C116, C141) is strongly supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches across both anti-amyloid and antiviral activities. The combination of negative controls (alanine substitution), competition experiments, BSA/centrifugation controls, dose-response analysis, and biophysical characterization provides robust support for the specific lysine/arginine-binding mechanism.

results.result: CLR01 counteracts both host factors (seminal amyloids) and the pathogen (HIV) itself through dual mechanisms operating on different timescales: rapid viral membrane disruption (minutes) and slower amyloid inhibition/remodeling (hours). The combined anti-amyloid and antiviral activities, along with minimal toxicity and efficacy in seminal fluid, make CLR01 a promising broad-spectrum topical microbicide for HIV-1 and other sexually transmitted viruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C22, C153, C169, C173-C177 represent the major conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data demonstrating: (1) inhibition and remodeling of seminal amyloids, (2) direct antiviral activity against multiple enveloped viruses, (3) lack of cytotoxicity, (4) efficacy in seminal plasma, and (5) specific lysine/arginine-dependent mechanisms. The dual mechanism and different timescales are clearly demonstrated. However, the designation as "promising" for clinical development is appropriately cautious given this is in vitro work.

results.result: Previous topical microbicide failures have been attributed to lack of adherence, adverse effects, and diminished efficacy in semen. Biological polyanions like heparin can prevent cationic fibrils from enhancing HIV infection but have been unsuccessful in clinical trials due to poor bioavailability and induction of inflammatory responses that recruit HIV-susceptible cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C152 accurately summarize prior work on microbicide failures and are supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for why CLR01's dual mechanism and lack of inflammatory effects might overcome previous limitations.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence argue against a non-specific colloidal mechanism: CLR01's anti-amyloid and antiviral activities are unaffected by high BSA concentrations or centrifugation; alanine substitution abolishes activity on both fibrils and assembly; antiviral activity is restricted to enveloped viruses; and excess lysine/poly-L-lysine eliminates both activities.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C159 from the Discussion accurately summarize the experimental evidence against colloidal mechanisms. These claims are well-supported by the data presented throughout the Results section and provide appropriate interpretation of the findings.

results.result: CLR01's selectivity arises from its binding properties: it only disrupts weak interactions and events depending on accessible lysine/arginine residues. Inhibition of abnormal protein aggregation requires ~1:1-1:5 protein:CLR01, while disruption of controlled polymerization requires ~55-fold excess and enzyme inhibition requires ~1000-fold excess. In vivo, CLR01 shows no toxicity at doses 2-3 orders of magnitude above those needed for amyloid clearance. The lysine-rich nature of seminal amyloids makes them unusually sensitive to CLR01, with sub-stoichiometric concentrations sufficient for inhibition and remodeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C166 provide mechanistic interpretation supported by the current data and prior literature. The differential sensitivity based on lysine/arginine accessibility and the sub-stoichiometric activity are well-demonstrated. The safety data from prior in vivo studies are appropriately cited.

results.result: CLR01 may possess similarities to other broad-spectrum antivirals like LJ001 that selectively disrupt viral membranes but not cell membranes or non-enveloped viruses. HSV-2, HCMV, and HCV can be transmitted via sexual intercourse.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C168 make appropriate comparisons to related compounds and accurately state that these viruses can be sexually transmitted, supported by citations. These claims provide useful context for understanding CLR01's mechanism and potential applications.

results.result: CLR01 showed no cytotoxicity in this study and has been safely employed in multiple cell and animal models. Transgenic mice given 10 mg/kg/day CLR01 intraperitoneally for 30 days showed no apparent toxicity or adverse effects. Application on mucosal surfaces should be even safer than systemic administration.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 are supported by the current cytotoxicity data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and prior in vivo studies (appropriately cited). The inference that topical application might be safer than systemic administration (C172) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Large-scale synthesis of CLR01 could be relatively inexpensive (less than $1 per mg), enabling development as a broad-spectrum antiviral microbicide.
results.evaluation: Claim C178 is speculative about future manufacturing costs without supporting data or analysis. While the authors may have informal estimates, no evidence is provided to support the specific cost projection of <$1/mg at scale.
